title: Frobenius on finite fields
text: We describe the \(q\)-power Frobenius on finite fields and identify its fixed points.

title: Frobenius on finite fields
text:
The Frobenius automorphism
Let \(q=p^r\) be a prime power. In any field of characteristic \(p\),
\[
(a+b)^p=a^p+b^p,
\]
because the intermediate binomial coefficients are divisible by \(p\). Iterating gives the same identity for the \(q\)th power.
On \(K=\mathbb F_{q^n}\), the map \(F_q(a)=a^q\) is therefore a field homomorphism. It is injective, hence bijective because \(K\) is finite. It fixes \(\mathbb F_q\) pointwise.

title: Frobenius on finite fields
text:
The fixed field

Proposition 1 (Fixed field of the q-power map) The fixed elements of \(F_q\) in \(\mathbb F_{q^n}\) are exactly \(\mathbb F_q\).


Proof. Every element of \(\mathbb F_q\) satisfies \(a^q=a\). Conversely, fixed elements are roots of \(T^q-T\), a polynomial of degree \(q\), so there are at most \(q\) of them. The \(q\) elements already found exhaust the possibilities.

For example, write \(\mathbb F_4=\mathbb F_2(\alpha)\) with \(\alpha^2+\alpha+1=0\). Squaring interchanges \(\alpha\) and \(\alpha+1\), and fixes \(0\) and \(1\).

title: Frobenius on finite fields
text:
Rational points
Suppose an affine variety is defined by polynomial equations with coefficients in \(\mathbb F_q\). Raising every coordinate of a solution in \(\overline{\mathbb F}_q\) to the \(q\)th power produces another solution.
A geometric point is fixed by this operation precisely when every coordinate lies in \(\mathbb F_q\). Thus rational points can be recognized as fixed points of a Frobenius action. For example,
\[
\mathbb A^1(\mathbb F_q)
=\{a\in\overline{\mathbb F}_q:a^q=a\}.
\]






NoteFrobenius conventions



On \(\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), the automorphism \(a\mapsto a^q\) is called arithmetic Frobenius. Its inverse is called geometric Frobenius. This note uses the arithmetic convention throughout; the distinction matters when comparing cohomological formulas.

title: Maschke’s theorem via averaging
text: We prove Maschke’s theorem by averaging a linear projection over a finite group.

title: Maschke’s theorem via averaging
text:
The averaged projection
Let \(G\) be a finite group and \(V\) a finite-dimensional representation over a field \(k\) in which \(|G|\) is invertible. Let \(W\subseteq V\) be a \(G\)-stable subspace.
Linear algebra gives a projection \(P:V\to W\) that restricts to the identity on \(W\). But its kernel need not be \(G\)-stable. Average its conjugates:
\[
\overline P=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}gPg^{-1}.
\tag{1}\]
Each summand maps into \(W\) and restricts to the identity there. The same is true of \(\overline P\).

title: Maschke’s theorem via averaging
text:
Equivariance and complete reducibility
For any \(h\in G\), multiplication by \(h\) permutes the group elements. Reindexing Equation 1 therefore gives
\[
h\overline P h^{-1}
=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}(hg)P(hg)^{-1}
=\overline P.
\]
So \(\overline P\) is \(G\)-equivariant, and its kernel is a \(G\)-stable complement to \(W\).

Theorem 1 (Maschke’s theorem) If \(G\) is finite and \(\operatorname{char}k\) does not divide \(|G|\), every finite-dimensional representation of \(G\) over \(k\) is a direct sum of irreducible representations.


Proof. For a nonzero representation, choose a nonzero invariant subspace of smallest positive dimension; it is irreducible. The averaged projection supplies an invariant complement. Induction on dimension completes the decomposition.

title: Maschke’s theorem via averaging
text:
A counterexample in characteristic p
In characteristic \(p\), consider a cyclic group of order \(p\) acting on \(k^2\) by the matrix
\[
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Writing \(T=I+N\) with \(N^2=0\) shows \(T^p=I\). The line \(ke_1\) is invariant, but has no invariant complementary line. Indeed, a complementary line would have a generator \(ae_1+be_2\) with \(b\ne0\). Its image is \((a+b)e_1+be_2\); proportionality forces the scalar to be \(1\) and then forces \(b=0\), a contradiction.
The missing factor \(1/|G|\) is not merely a problem with the proof: the conclusion can fail.

title: Hartogs’ principle and Serre’s S₂ condition
text: Let \(X\) be a Noetherian scheme satisfying \(S_2\). We consider extension of regular functions from the complement of a closed subset of codimension at least two.

title: Hartogs’ principle and Serre’s S₂ condition
text:
The punctured affine plane
Let \(k\) be a field, set \(A=k[x,y]\), and remove the origin from \(X=\operatorname{Spec}A\). The resulting open set is
\[
U=D(x)\cup D(y).
\]
A regular function on \(U\) is a pair of functions in \(A_x\) and \(A_y\) that agree in \(A_{xy}\). Since these rings embed in \(k(x,y)\), we can identify
\[
\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)=A_x\cap A_y=A.
\tag{1}\]
Why is the intersection just \(A\)? A denominator that is both a power of \(x\) and a power of \(y\) must cancel: unique factorization and the coprimality of \(x\) and \(y\) force the rational function to be a polynomial. Removing the origin has introduced no new regular functions.

title: Hartogs’ principle and Serre’s S₂ condition
text:
The depth condition
A Noetherian ring \(A\) satisfies Serre’s condition \(S_2\) if, for every prime ideal \(\mathfrak p\),
\[
\operatorname{depth} A_{\mathfrak p}
\geq \min\{2,\dim A_{\mathfrak p}\}.
\]
Here is an affine formulation that makes the codimension hypothesis explicit.

Theorem 1 (Algebraic Hartogs principle) Let \(A\) be a Noetherian ring satisfying \(S_2\), and let \(I\subseteq A\) be an ideal such that \(\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p\geq2\) for every prime \(\mathfrak p\) containing \(I\). If \(U=\operatorname{Spec}A\setminus V(I)\), restriction gives an isomorphism
\[
A\xrightarrow{\sim}\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U).
\]

The height condition says exactly which local rings must have depth at least two. It avoids any ambiguity about codimension when components have different dimensions.

title: Hartogs’ principle and Serre’s S₂ condition
text:
Proof using local cohomology

Proof. The local cohomology sequence begins
\[
\begin{aligned}
0\longrightarrow H_I^0(A)\longrightarrow A
&\longrightarrow\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)\\
&\longrightarrow H_I^1(A)\longrightarrow0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}\]
For every \(\mathfrak p\in V(I)\), the hypotheses give \(\operatorname{depth}A_{\mathfrak p}\geq2\). The depth criterion for local cohomology therefore gives \(H_I^0(A)=H_I^1(A)=0\). Exactness of Equation 2 proves the claim.

The two vanishings have different jobs: \(H_I^0(A)=0\) gives uniqueness of extension, while \(H_I^1(A)=0\) gives existence.
Applying Theorem 1 on affine open subsets and gluing gives the scheme version: for a Noetherian \(S_2\) scheme \(X\) and a closed subset \(Z\) with \(\dim\mathcal O_{X,z}\geq2\) at every \(z\in Z\),
\[
\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)\xrightarrow{\sim}
\Gamma(X\setminus Z,\mathcal O_X).
\]

title: Hartogs’ principle and Serre’s S₂ condition
text:
A codimension-one counterexample
Remove the origin from the affine line instead. Now
\[
\Gamma(\mathbb A_k^1\setminus\{0\},\mathcal O)
=k[t,t^{-1}],
\]
which contains \(t^{-1}\). This function cannot extend across the origin. The codimension bound in Theorem 1 is doing real work.

title: Hartogs’ principle and Serre’s S₂ condition
